newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Troubled Cambodia seeks 'oases' of investment.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Cambodia seeks 'oases' of investment.

text.p: Iaian Gray, president of Malaysia-based Dragon Gold chose an interesting week to seal a $3.4 billion investment in Cambodia.

Thousands of garment workers took to the streets to protest their working conditions, political tensions simmered in the capital and Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad raised concerns about the country's stability.

But Gray was undeterred, in part because he believes his planned regional air cargo hub and 12,500-hectare, (30,000-acre) self-contained industrial zone can be viewed as separate from the country's uneasy environment.
"Although the site is Cambodia, this is not necessarily a Cambodian project. It's a global airport that happens to be in Cambodia," he said in an interview with Reuters.

In fact, with political tensions grabbing headlines and investor concern over poor infrastructure and instability at a high, Gray's concept is becoming Cambodia's biggest selling point, said analysts.

Government officials, fed up with short-term, quick-profit investors that flow in to Cambodia, are trying to lure long-term business with the idea of economic oases -- development zones with self-contained, modern infrastructure and few domestic controls, near the country's ports, railways and airports.
It's not unlike living in Cambodia without ever going there, said analysts.

"The industrial zone is the right thing to do. It's what you can call a clean zone, with infrastructure there, water treatment, industry, telecommunications, highways, warehouses in the location. So investors come, and everything is there," said Chanthol Sun, secretary-general of the Council for the Development of Cambodia (CDC).

The CDC, set up in 1994, seeks to provide investors with a one-stop, fast-track route to business opportunities in Cambodia. Despite a year of ups and downs, it has succeeded in approving more than $1 billion investment in 1996, not including the recent Kompong Chhnang airport deal, said Chanthol Sun.
Many future projects are built around the "oasis" concept.

In addition to the Kompong Chhnang project, which will have an "open skies" policy for aircraft and upgraded infrastructure, Japan-based Marubeni Corp is considering a large industrial zone at the southern port of Sihanoukville.

A "model city" concept is in the works for the seaside town of Koh Kong, and Hong Kong-based Sun Wah Group has purchased 10 hectares (25 acres) of land for a $50 million industrial project near Phnom Penh's Pochentong airport.
A large industrial zone for garment factories, one of the country's booming sectors with 34 factories and 16,000 workres, is also planned for Phnom Penh.

While the idea of few domestic controls, free trade and insulation from poor infrastructure appeal to investors, some express concern that isolated projects will not benefit war-torn Cambodia's tiny tax base and long-term rehabilitation.

"If you have self-contained zones, there is less competition here and less benefit to Cambodians. We need to look after the interests of our people," said Kao Kim Hourn of the Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace.
But he expressed support for "sustainable, long-term investment from committed investors who train workers and don't necessarily expect a quick return".

To pull in that type of company, the CDC offers a long list of investment incentives: nine percent corporate income tax, tax holidays of up to eight years, full import duty exemptions for export-oriented projects, free repatriation of profits and no nationalisation or price controls.
Overall, it's a package Cambodia hopes will more than compensate for political woes, run-down infrastructure and a lack of legal framework that lies just outside the oases.
"Investors should consider Cambodia seriously. Yes, there are political tensions lately, but that's a black cloud over our head that we hope will soon go away," said Chanthol Sun.
"Cambodia makes sense in the long term."
